content.title: Three applications under one name
content.body: The fields on this page point at a specific product: the name Affinity, the category Design & Creative, the website affinity.serif.com, and a tagline describing a professional graphic design software suite. The repository's freelancer hub names what sits inside that suite — Affinity Designer, Photo, and Publisher, each offered one-time with no subscription. Nothing written here comes from anyone using the software; the description is assembled from this repository's guides, category pages, and comparison files, together with the fields stored on this page. One caution applies to everything below: the comparison data around this product does not always treat it as the purchased design suite its own fields describe.

content.title: Photo editing as the recorded use case
content.body: The clearest functional description in the repository appears in the design-software guide: a team that primarily uses one or two Adobe applications is told to evaluate whether a specialized alternative would serve its needs at lower cost and with a shallower learning curve, and the three examples given are Figma for UI, Affinity for photo editing, and DaVinci Resolve for video. That sentence does two jobs at once — it records photo editing as Affinity's recognized strength, and it positions the product as a substitute for part of a design workflow rather than for the whole of one. The freelancer hub adds the commercial version of the same argument by recording all three applications at one-time prices.

content.title: Four records, four different answers on price
content.body: This page's own fields record Affinity as paid with a one-time band of $69.99, and every comparison record attached to the product repeats that figure as its starting price. Three other records in the repository describe the same commercial model with different amounts attached, and none of them agrees with the band above. Because the dataset holds no single confirmed current list price for Affinity, those figures are summarized rather than repeated here, and the vendor's own address — recorded on this page as affinity.serif.com — is where the question gets settled. The disagreement itself is worth recording:
items: This page's fields, with a paid model and a one-time band of $69.99
The freelancer hub, recording Designer, Photo, and Publisher at one-time prices with no subscription
The design category page, recording a one-time band per application with free updates
The small-business ranking, recording Designer as a one-time purchase option

content.title: What a purchase model implies, and what it omits
content.body: A perpetual license with free updates, which is what the category page records, changes the shape of the decision: cost sits in the purchase rather than in an annual line, and no renewal date forces a re-evaluation. It also removes the levers a subscription buyer would use — there is no plan to downgrade and no seat count to move mid-year — so the commitment is made once for each application. Beyond the commercial shape, this repository records little about daily use of the suite: no workflow descriptions, no file-format notes, no collaboration features, and no integration or ecosystem entries appear anywhere in the records held for Affinity, so those questions stay open on this page.

content.title: How the comparison pages place Affinity
content.body: Ten comparison records in this repository pair Affinity with something else, and the field is uneven. The rows place it ahead of Adobe Express, Adobe XD, Canva, CircleCI, ConvertKit, InVision, Sketch, Wix, and Zeplin, and behind Figma — with starting price marked in its favor only against Canva, whose model is subscription-based. Two of those pairings are category mismatches by this repository's own labels: CircleCI is a build service and ConvertKit is an email tool, yet both are recorded against a design suite. The alternatives pages repeat that grouping from the other direction, listing Framer, Webflow, InVision, and Zeplin as Affinity's alternatives.

content.title: Ratings that do not agree with each other
content.body: The rating on this page is 4.6 out of 5 from 1,300 reviews, and that figure is the one attached to every comparison record here — Affinity carries the highest rating in its comparison field apart from Figma at 4.8. Four other pages in the repository list the same product among their alternatives at 4 out of 5 instead, which means a reader moving between pages meets two different aggregates for one name. No source in the dataset explains the difference. Where records conflict like this, this page keeps its own figure and flags the other rather than picking a winner, and a reader should treat cross-page rating comparisons as approximate.

content.title: Who the design guides point at
content.body: The recorded positioning is substitution rather than expansion: the design guide recommends Affinity when a team already working in one or two Adobe applications wants a specialized tool for photo editing, and it frames the trade in terms of lower cost and a shallower learning curve. Our freelancer hub files the three applications as professional alternatives at one-time prices, which makes the audience individuals and small studios rather than procurement-led teams. The comparison field reinforces that reading — the products Affinity is measured against are mostly design and web tools, with Figma the one it trails. An organization already standardized on a subscription design platform has little recorded reason here to switch.

content.title: Delivery, updates, and the certification gap
content.body: What the repository establishes for Affinity is commercial rather than operational: a perpetual license per application, free updates alongside it, and a one-time purchase instead of a subscription. How the software is delivered, where files live while it is open, and whether any collaboration happens through a hosted service are not recorded here, so this page makes no claim about them. The same silence covers compliance: no certification of any kind is stored with this product's records, and nothing on this page should be read as evidence that a standard is met or missed. A buyer working through a security or deployment questionnaire needs the vendor's current documentation for those answers.

content.title: Where this suite fits
content.body: Taken together, the records describe a purchased graphic design suite of three applications, strongest in photo editing, sold one-time with free updates, and rated 4.6 out of 5 from 1,300 reviews on this page. It fits an individual designer or a small studio that prefers a committed purchase to an annual renewal and does not need an integration or collaboration layer that our records cannot confirm. It fits poorly where a buyer must see integrations, file formats, or a confirmed current price before signing, because the dataset holds none of those to a single answer. The open items here are the price disagreement and the rating discrepancy, both of which should be settled with the vendor and this repository's own pages respectively.

faqs.question: Which applications make up Affinity?
faqs.answer: The freelancer hub names three: Affinity Designer, Photo, and Publisher, each offered one-time with no subscription, while the design category page describes a perpetual license per application with free updates.

faqs.question: Is Affinity sold as a subscription?
faqs.answer: No. This page records a paid model with a one-time band of $69.99, the category page records a perpetual license with free updates, and the freelancer hub states the applications carry no subscription.

faqs.question: Why do the price records for Affinity disagree?
faqs.answer: Four pages in this repository record the same commercial model with different amounts, so no current list price is confirmed here; the vendor address stored on this page, affinity.serif.com, is where to settle it.

faqs.question: What is Affinity recommended for in this repository?
faqs.answer: Photo editing. The design guide suggests it as the specialized option for teams running one or two Adobe applications, framed around lower cost and a shallower learning curve.

faqs.question: How does Affinity compare against other design tools here?
faqs.answer: Ten comparison records place it ahead of Adobe Express, Adobe XD, Canva, CircleCI, ConvertKit, InVision, Sketch, Wix, and Zeplin, and behind Figma, while its alternatives page names Framer, Webflow, InVision, and Zeplin.

author: Emily Nakamura
learningCurve: Steep — requires dedicated training time for full proficiency
whoShouldUse: Individual designers and small studios that want a purchased design suite rather than an annual renewal, especially where photo editing is the specific job and Adobe applications already cover the rest of the workflow.
whoShouldNotUse: Buyers who need recorded integrations, collaboration features, file formats, or a confirmed current price before deciding — none of which this repository's records establish for Affinity.
